implementation_notes: pact-jvm supplies both halves of the pattern on the JVM. On the consumer side @ExtendWith(PactConsumerTestExt.class) (or @PactConsumerTest) plus a @Pact method returning RequestResponsePact builds the interactions with the PactDslWithProvider/PactDslJsonBody DSL (stringType, eachLike, minArrayLike, matchUrl, timestamp, ...), and @PactTestFor(providerName = ...) starts one mock server per test and can inject its MockServer into the test method; contracts are written to target/pacts by default and pact.rootDir overrides that. Provider verification uses the matching pact-jvm provider module, which replays the contracts against the running service and, with a broker configured, feeds the deployability decision.
pitfalls: HTTP keep-alive defeats per-test mock servers: a client reusing a pooled connection can hit the closed mock server of the previous test, so disable keep-alive or make the mock server send Connection: close.
Pact files in target/pacts are merged with what is already there; a stale interaction keeps being verified unless the build cleans the directory or pact.writer.overwrite is set.
pact.rootDir is read by the forked test JVM, so it must be configured (surefire systemPropertyVariables, Gradle systemProperties, sbt javaOptions) or the publish step finds nothing.
The mock server binds inside the test JVM and only localhost/127.0.0.1/::1 (or the machine's own host name) are valid bind addresses for it.

variants.name: Spring Cloud Contract (declarative contract DSL, generated stubs)
variants.implementation_notes: Spring Cloud Contract inverts the mechanics: the interaction is declared as a contract (Groovy DSL, YAML, Java or Kotlin DSL) which the build plugin compiles into WireMock stubs the consumer tests against and into a generated provider-side verification test that replays the same contract against the real service - the contract file, not the consumer test, is the source of truth. It supports consumer-driven and producer-driven workflows, and is usually the pragmatic choice when the provider is a Spring Boot application whose build already runs the plugin; the cost is that the consumer no longer produces its own contract as a by-product.
pitfalls: Stubs and generated verification tests are build outputs: a consumer test running against a stale generated stub keeps passing while the contract has already changed.
Editing the contract means regenerating both sides, so the consumer test is no longer the artifact that defines what the consumer needs - keep one owner per contract or the two representations drift.
JSON body matchers (bodyMatchers/jsonPath) must be declared explicitly; without them the whole body is compared exactly and harmless provider additions fail verification.
